item.title: The Town Council Race Was Tied. The Three of Spades Called It.
item.description:
There was an old-fashioned Wild West standoff this week in a onetime frontier outpost.

Two candidates for Town Council in Gila Bend, Ariz., finished with the same number of votes in July’s election, 67 each. A century-old state law mandated breaking the tie with a game of chance.

In this duel, there would be no gunslinging, though there would be a draw — not from a holster, but from a shuffled deck of cards. The hopeful with the higher card would claim the seat.

In an age of increasing distrust in elections and a state that has been a hotbed for voting-related conspiracy theories, Gila Bend’s leaders said they knew the high-stakes tiebreaker, which took place Tuesday, would need to be transparent and carefully choreographed.

“With everything that’s going on, you want it as open as you can possibly get it,” said Patricia Riggs, the town clerk, who oversees elections.

The stalemate in this 1,800-person community, 50 miles southwest of Phoenix, was hardly the first to be decided by chance in a country with tens of thousands of elected local governments and closely divided politics. Races in recent decades have come down to poker games, straw-drawing and, earlier this month in Hawaii, names tucked into plastic eggs and picked from a woven basket.

But Gila Bend’s tie might have been the first involving a candidate who had been in the exact same position years before. Jesus Rubalcava finished neck and neck with an opponent in 2014 and won his first term on the Council with the flip of a $1 coin.

After a court-certified recount earlier this month confirmed his deadlock with the newcomer Athena Guerrero, Ms. Riggs informed Mr. Rubalcava that his election fate would once again come down to chance.

Did that make him lucky or unlucky? Mr. Rubalcava, a high school teacher and former state legislator, wasn’t sure.

“I was in disbelief,” he said. “I couldn’t wrap my head around it.”

It was up to Ms. Riggs and other town officials to choose what form the rubber match would take. Arizona law stipulated only that the tie be broken “by lot.” They ruled out rock-paper-scissors, and they opted against drawing marbles or straws.

“We thought that was kind of boring,” Ms. Riggs said.

High-card draw would be more exciting, they decided, and it would be easy for the public to understand and follow.

Ms. Guerrero was initially wary. “I’m not a gambling type of person,” she said.

But she knew enough to pray for an ace. Ms. Guerrero, who works for a water treatment plant, had long eyed politics, and she imagined the Town Council as a launching pad. Eventually, she said, she would like to be mayor.

Gila Bend, an important stop on a storied 19th-century stagecoach line, is now a manufacturing and farming town where local politics is unavoidably personal. In separate interviews, Ms. Guerrero and Mr. Rubalcava each said they “have nothing but love” for the other.

Neither campaigned aggressively, and the nail-biter was a reminder that every vote counts. Mr. Rubalcava’s mother, brother and niece all failed to cast ballots, he said.

They were not alone. Fewer than 200 of the town’s roughly 600 registered voters participated in the July election.

Ms. Riggs spent three weeks painstakingly planning Tuesday’s showdown, consulting with lawyers and election experts. She devised a list of 19 steps that documented exactly how the draw would go, and she wrote a script to read while she conducted it.

On Tuesday morning, she borrowed a mechanical card shuffler from her sister-in-law and bought two decks at the town’s Dollar General, one for practice. That night, the two candidates sidled up to a table in a school building and exchanged nervous smiles in front of a handful of residents and the sitting Council members.

Ms. Riggs stated the rules, opened and spread a new deck of cards and let Ms. Guerrero and Mr. Rubalcava inspect them. She shuffled and presented the stack to Ms. Guerrero, who cut it. Mr. Rubalcava then cut it again.

The candidates were reminded that, in the event they drew the same number — like that would ever happen — spades would trump other suits.

Ms. Riggs pulled Ms. Guerrero’s card first, a three of clubs. The candidate sighed.

Ms. Riggs flipped Mr. Rubalcava’s card next.

Another three, another tie. The audience gasped. Mr. Rubacalva couldn’t believe it. “Did this really just happen?” he thought.

But his three was a spade, delivering Mr. Rubalcava a chance victory for the second time. The candidates laughed and shook hands.

“Who would have thought?” a stunned Ms. Riggs said to the room.

Ms. Guerrero said on Wednesday that she planned to run for office again, pledging to “come back strong in a couple years.”

Ms. Riggs said she was glad to hear it, then added: “God forbid there’s a tie.”

item.title: With Term Winding Down, Pelosi Tries to Anoint a Successor
item.description:
Nancy Pelosi has a meaty to-do list in her final months in office: Ensure Democrats take back the House of Representatives. Fend off attempts by the Trump administration to make it harder to vote in the midterms.

And persuade San Franciscans to send a local elected leader little known outside the city to replace her in Washington.

Ms. Pelosi, 86, who is finishing her final term in Congress after representing San Francisco since 1987, has never been one to sit back and watch politics play out. This particular campaign is no exception.

She has engaged in the race to a surprising degree, considering that she did not seem to have longstanding ties with her preferred candidate, Connie Chan, a member of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors. Still, Ms. Pelosi has publicly inserted herself in the race and has worked vigorously behind the scenes to get Ms. Chan elected.

Ms. Chan and her opponent, State Senator Scott Wiener, will square off Nov. 3 in an intraparty battle. Like most San Franciscans, both candidates are liberal Democrats and share a disdain for the Trump administration, as well as a desire to expand rights for immigrants and gay and transgender people.

But they represent different camps in the city’s combative political scene, particularly on housing. Mr. Wiener, 56, has gained national attention as a prolific state legislator focused on getting as much housing as possible built. Ms. Chan, 47, has a reputation in San Francisco for regularly blocking housing proposals, which she sees as lining the pockets of developers to the detriment of low-income tenants who could be displaced.

He calls her an obstructionist best known for voting “no,” saying she is trying to keep San Francisco frozen in amber. She calls him beholden to corporations and billionaires.

Enter Ms. Pelosi.

The first woman to serve as the speaker of the House, she stayed out of the primary campaign until the final two weeks, when she endorsed Ms. Chan. Since then, she has hosted a fund-raiser in the Jackson Square neighborhood for Ms. Chan, lent her communications director to Ms. Chan’s campaign and worked the phones to gather endorsements, including an unsuccessful attempt to convince the labor leader Dolores Huerta to endorse both candidates, not just Mr. Wiener.

Mr. Wiener’s camp believes Ms. Pelosi has been motivated less by wanting to elevate Ms. Chan than by seeking to block him from the seat he has long coveted. It was well known in California political circles that he had been eyeing Ms. Pelosi’s seat for years, and he had once vowed not to run until she announced her retirement.

Last October, however, Mr. Wiener refused to wait any longer and jumped into the race before Ms. Pelosi announced her decision.

Ms. Pelosi has given few interviews about the congressional race. But she said this week that her support for Ms. Chan had nothing to do with her feelings about Mr. Wiener.

“Nobody knows Congress better than I do. Nobody,” Ms. Pelosi said. “And I think she would be the best member of Congress.”

Ms. Pelosi answered questions about the race after an event at San Francisco City Hall to herald the 106th anniversary of the certification of the 19th Amendment, which established the right to vote for women.

There, she listed several reasons for her involvement: Ms. Chan is a woman at a time when women are losing political power. The two have long ties to the city’s powerful labor unions. Ms. Chan performed well as the chairwoman of the board’s budget committee. And Ms. Chan worked hard to help pass Proposition 50, the 2025 ballot measure that gerrymandered California’s congressional map to the benefit of Democrats in response to a similar move in Texas that aided Republicans.

The only negative word Ms. Pelosi would say this week about Mr. Wiener was to reiterate her anger over a satirical chatbot his campaign created that was intended to parrot Ms. Chan and always say “no.”

The stunt backfired when supporters of Ms. Chan, who moved to San Francisco from Hong Kong when she was 13, typed in topics not related to policies, such as the word “accent.” The bot responded with lines that included, “I’m afraid my San Francisco accent is so thick I can barely understand myself.”

Ms. Pelosi released an open letter co-signed by numerous San Francisco female politicians and political groups saying that the chatbot relied on “racist, misogynist tropes for cheap political points.” Mr. Wiener apologized and took the chatbot down.

A group of prominent women who support Mr. Wiener held a rally last weekend in Alamo Square to denounce what they viewed as false outrage over the chatbot and promote his record of legislation important to women, including to expand reproductive freedom and health care access.

Susie Tompkins Buell, founder of the Esprit clothing company and a Democratic power broker in California, spoke at the rally and said in an interview later that she was confused about why Ms. Pelosi was going all-in for a less experienced candidate.

“It’s not about any woman. It’s about the right woman,” she said. “Connie Chan is a place where progress goes to die.”

This week, Ms. Pelosi said she held no ill will against Mr. Wiener for anything other than the chatbot.

“I haven’t said anything about her opponent except when he tried to put words in the mouth of a woman, which is something that I have been fighting to protect my whole career,” Ms. Pelosi said.

Some in San Francisco political circles have speculated that Ms. Pelosi was frustrated with Mr. Wiener because his candidacy might have edged out her own daughter, Christine Pelosi, from running for her seat. But Ms. Pelosi said this week that she and her daughter had never talked about a succession plan; Christine Pelosi is now running to fill Mr. Wiener’s seat in the State Senate.

“She wants to have her own path in California, which I love,” Ms. Pelosi said. “There was never any thought that she would run for my seat, although they like to use that because they don’t know what they’re talking about.”

Christine Pelosi, who was at the City Hall event wearing a tiny pin of a famous image of her mother in a red coat and sunglasses, reiterated that she had never planned to run for Congress and added that she, too, was supporting Ms. Chan. “With respect, some of us do things for positive reasons,” Christine Pelosi said.

In an interview, Ms. Chan said she and Ms. Pelosi have talked often in recent months, and that the congresswoman has been generous with her advice. Ms. Chan described filming the endorsement video together as a pinch-me moment.

“Deep inside me, I was thinking, ‘Oh, I only wish my mother was still alive to see this,’” she said.

Mr. Wiener said in an interview that the chatter about Ms. Pelosi’s involvement was a distraction.

“I’m not running against Nancy Pelosi. I’m running against Connie Chan,” he said. “And I’m going to win.”

item.title: Jury Deliberations Underway in Lindsay Clancy Murder Trial
item.description:
Jury deliberations are set to resume on Friday morning in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman charged with murder for strangling her three young children in 2023.

After more than four weeks of often emotional testimony in the high-profile case, the lawyers on each side made their closing arguments at the courthouse in Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday. It was their final opportunity to convince the jurors whether or not Ms. Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the children’s deaths.

Ms. Clancy does not deny that she killed the children at her home in Duxbury, Mass., an affluent Boston suburb, and has pursued an insanity defense. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, maintains that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and had experienced auditory hallucinations of a man’s voice ordering her to kill her children and then herself.

Mr. Reddington described Ms. Clancy on Thursday as “a darn good mother” and a respected nurse who loved her children. He read from a long list of medications that had been prescribed to Ms. Clancy in the months before the killings, arguing that she had received “lousy medical care” when she sought help for her anxiety.

“This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children,” Mr. Reddington said, “because she was suffering from a disease and defect.”

Earlier on Thursday, the judge, William Sullivan of Plymouth County Superior Court, had told the jurors that Ms. Clancy could not be held criminally responsible if she had a mental disease or defect that prevented her from controlling her actions, or from distinguishing right from wrong.

Jennifer Sprague, a prosecutor, used her closing argument to present the killings as a series of rationally made and premeditated choices. She called the killings an act of “extreme atrocity and cruelty” and described the horrific scene that Ms. Clancy had left behind.

“She left them discarded on the basement floor, like broken toys, because she was done playing the game,” Ms. Sprague said. “You know, to a moral certainty, she is guilty.”

Prosecutors have argued that Ms. Clancy plotted to get her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, out of the house on Jan. 24, 2023. Mr. Clancy returned home from picking up takeout food to find the children in the basement with exercise bands around their necks, he said during his testimony. Cora, 5, and Dawson, 3, were dead. Callan, 8 months, died days later.

Mr. Clancy also found Ms. Clancy lying injured in the backyard. She had cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window of the home in what her lawyers have called a suicide attempt, which left her partially paralyzed.

Ms. Clancy, 36, did not testify during the trial. The witnesses have included Ms. Clancy’s mother, her sister, her former mother-in-law, and several psychologists who treated Ms. Clancy before the killings or evaluated her afterward. The prosecution rested early last week after calling more than 70 witnesses, and the defense rested on Friday after calling 10.

Rebuttals, which give prosecutors an opportunity to respond to claims made by the defense, took up the last few days of the trial. The three rebuttal witnesses for the prosecution, all forensic psychologists, pointed to evidence that Ms. Clancy may not have been suffering from postpartum psychosis. In combative cross-examinations, Mr. Reddington questioned their expertise and at one point asked the judge to grant a mistrial after one of the witnesses mentioned the concept of “mortal sin” while discussing Ms. Clancy’s Catholic upbringing.

For much of the trial, a crowd of demonstrators has gathered outside the courtroom. Many were women who wore pink to support Ms. Clancy and to call attention to what they see as the health care system’s failures to address maternal mental health.

In her closing argument, Ms. Sprague said that the case was “not about our mental health system, or how it treats women.”

She added: “That’s a distraction to get you angry and passionate — about an important issue, but an issue that’s not on trial here.”

To secure a guilty verdict, the prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Ms. Clancy committed the crime, knew that the murders were wrong and had some control over her actions.

Judge Sullivan instructed the jury to choose among first-degree murder, second-degree murder and manslaughter if they find Ms. Clancy guilty. She faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder.
